terms.gloss: wrong, not to be done; a wrong
terms.grammar: noun, indeclinable; nefās est with an infinitive, it is wrong to
evidence: Cic. Fam. 15.21.5: quae cum tibi liceat, mihi nefās sit oblīvīscī
Cic. Att. 9.2a.1: quam sit turpe mē adesse … nefās esse approbāre
terms.comment: What the gods and decency forbid; its opposite is fās, and right and wrong together are fās atque nefās. A strong word, though Cicero uses it freely in his letters; milder is turpe est, it is shameful.

evidence: Cic. Ac. 1.37: rēctē facta sōla in bonīs āctiōnibus pōnēns, prāvē id est peccāta in malīs
terms.comment: Literally “crooked”. The adverb prāvē, wrongly, is the opposite of rēctē (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: a wrong done to someone, an injustice
evidence: Ter. Ad. 189: tamen tibi ā mē nūlla orta est injūria
terms.comment: To wrong someone is injūriam alicui facere (Cic. Fin. 3.71, Lewis & Short); the ablative injūriā is “wrongly, unjustly”.

evidence: Cic. Off. 1.23: injūstitiae duo genera sunt (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: tū velim tua in mē studia et officia multum tēcum recordēre. quae cum tibi liceat, mihi nefās sit oblīvīscī
phrases.english: I’d like you to think often of your goodness and kindness to me: you may forget them, but for me it would be wrong to

phrases.latin: quippe ubi fās versum atque nefās
phrases.english: for here right and wrong are turned upside down

phrases.latin: tamen tibi ā mē nūlla orta est injūria
phrases.english: and yet you have had no wrong from me

nefas.against: Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked; Traupman 409 nefas
nefas.html: Fās with the negative ne-. De Vaan 203, s.v. fās: from *bʰeh₂-os, “saying”, the root of fārī and fāma.

sources: Lewis & Short: nefas · Lewis & Short: pravus · Lewis & Short: injuria
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 333, 409. Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), p. 203.
Cicero (letters, Academica, De finibus), Terence and Vergil checked against the Perseus Latin texts.
